title: Classification of materials

book.title: My Revision Notes: AQA A Level Design and Technology: Product Design

needs: Name the seven classifications of materials.
Define each classification and its sub-classifications.
Name specific materials in each classification.
Explain why thermoplastics can be recycled and thermosets can't.
Explain why modern materials are not smart materials.

doNow.q: Name the seven classifications of materials.
doNow.a: Metals, woods, polymers, papers and boards, composites, smart materials, modern materials.

doNow.q: Which kind of polymer springs back after being squashed?
What is the difference between hardness and toughness?
doNow.a: Hardness resists scratching and indentation; toughness absorbs an impact without fracturing.

doNow.q: What does an electrical insulator do?
doNow.a: It does not let electricity flow through it.

clues: When I'm heated, a chemical change locks my molecules together with rigid cross links.
Once I've set, no amount of heat will let you reshape me.

bigPicture.question: How do designers sort materials, and why does it matter?

chunks.label: Seven classifications
chunks.summary: Every product design material sits in one of seven groups.

items.ask: If you sorted every material in the workshop into groups, what groups would you use?
items.text: Metals, woods, polymers, papers and boards, composites, smart and modern materials.

image.alt: A spread of wood blocks, metal tubes, coloured plastic and card samples on a workshop bench.

items.ask: Is 'wood' just one group, or could you split it up further?
items.text: Metals, woods and polymers split again, as wood splits into hardwood, softwood and manufactured board.

image.alt: Three boards side by side on a bench: a darker plank, a pale pine plank and a layered plywood strip.

items.ask: Why does a designer need to know which group a material belongs to?
items.text: So the most suitable material can be chosen for each application.

image.alt: A designer at a studio desk with a computer, holding up one material sample from a row of swatches.

items.ask: In an exam answer, why might writing just 'metal' cost you marks?
items.text: Always name the exact material (low carbon steel), never just 'metal'.

check.q: Which three classifications split into sub-classifications?
Why should an exam answer say 'low carbon steel' rather than 'metal'?
check.a: Material questions need the specific material named, not just its classification.

items.ask: A magnet sticks to some metals but not others. What might those metals have in common?
items.text: Mostly iron and carbon; magnetic and will rust. E.g. low and medium carbon steel, cast iron.

image.alt: Two rusty steel bars looped together, lying on gravel.

items.ask: Why does a copper pipe never go rusty?
items.text: Contains no iron; not magnetic and won't rust. E.g. aluminium, copper, zinc, silver, gold, titanium, tin.

image.alt: Copper pipes running along a wall just below a wooden ceiling.

items.ask: Brass isn't dug out of the ground. How do you think it's made?
items.text: Two or more metals mixed, or elements combined where at least one is a metal.

image.alt: A stack of yellow brass ingots on a dark workbench in a metal workshop.

items.ask: Stainless steel is an alloy that contains iron. Which kind of alloy does that make it?
items.text: An alloy that contains iron, like stainless steel or die steel (tool steel).

image.alt: A set of polished stainless steel cutlery: a knife, two forks and two spoons.

items.ask: What would you call an alloy made without any iron, and can you name one?
items.text: An alloy with no iron, like bronze, brass, duralumin or pewter.

image.alt: A polished pewter tankard with a handle.

check.q: Give two ways ferrous metals differ from non-ferrous metals.
check.a: Ferrous metals contain iron (mostly iron and carbon), are magnetic and will rust; non-ferrous metals contain no iron, aren't magnetic and don't rust.

check.q: Name one ferrous alloy and one non-ferrous alloy.
check.a: Ferrous: stainless steel or die steel (tool steel). Non-ferrous: bronze, brass, duralumin or pewter.

items.ask: Think of a big leafy tree that goes bare every winter. What can you say about its timber?
items.text: From broad-leafed (deciduous) trees, generally slow growing. E.g. oak, ash, mahogany, teak, birch, beech.

image.alt: A tall stack of timber planks on bearers in a timber store, with a worker beside it.

items.ask: Christmas trees grow quickly and keep their needles all year. What kind of timber do they give?
items.text: From coniferous (cone-bearing) trees, generally fast growing and evergreen. E.g. pine, spruce, Douglas fir, redwood, cedar, larch.

image.alt: Stacks of felled logs beside a forest track lined with conifers.

items.ask: A tree trunk is only so wide. How could you get a wooden sheet bigger than any plank?
items.text: A man-made, wood-based composite, made in much larger sizes than solid wood. E.g. plywood, chipboard, MDF.

image.alt: A stack of plywood sheets on bearers in a joinery workshop.

check.q: What kind of tree does a softwood come from?
check.a: A coniferous (cone-bearing) tree, usually evergreen and fast growing.

check.q: Why can a manufactured board be used where solid wood is too small?
check.a: Manufactured boards are made in much larger sizes than solid wood.

items.ask: Why can an old plastic bottle be melted down and made into something new?
items.text: Can be reheated and reshaped again and again, so it can be recycled. E.g. LDPE, HDPE, PP, HIPS, ABS, PMMA, PET, nylon, PVC.

image.alt: A wire cage packed with used plastic drinks bottles.

items.ask: Why can't a melamine plate be melted down and moulded into something new?
items.text: A chemical change on heating forms rigid cross links, so it can't be reshaped. E.g. UF, MF, polyester and epoxy resin.

image.alt: A white melamine dinner plate with a floral border.

items.ask: What lets a squashed rubber ball spring straight back into shape?
items.text: Deforms under pressure at room temperature, then returns to its shape when released. E.g. natural rubber, polybutadiene, neoprene, silicone.

image.alt: A pile of brightly coloured rubber bouncy balls.

items.ask: What could be going on inside a polymer that lets it soften, set hard or stretch?
items.text: Thermoplastics have long linear chains held by van der Waals forces; elastomers have weak bonds, so they stretch.

image.alt: Three panels of polymer molecules labelled Thermoplastic, Thermosetting and Elastomer: separate chains, chains joined by cross links, and coiled chains.

items.ask: A product is meant to go in the recycling bin. Which kind of polymer should you never suggest?
items.text: Thermosetting polymers can't be recycled, so never choose one for a product that will be.

image.alt: A blue recycling wheelie bin next to a black bin on grass.

check.q: Why can a thermoplastic be recycled after its first use?
check.a: It can be reheated and reshaped again and again.

check.q: What happens to a thermosetting polymer's molecules when it is heated?
check.a: A chemical change makes them form rigid cross links, so it can't be reheated and reshaped.

chunks.label: Papers and boards
chunks.summary: Compliant materials, from layout paper to moulded pulp.

items.ask: Why is card so easy to turn into a box with just a knife, a ruler and some folds?
items.text: Can be scored, folded and cut with basic tools to make items such as packaging nets.

image.alt: An open, empty cardboard box standing on a wooden floor.

items.ask: How many different kinds of paper could you find in a designer's studio?
items.text: Layout, cartridge, tracing, bleed proof, treated and watercolour paper.

image.alt: Different papers laid out on a bench: tracing paper, sketches, watercolour and coloured sheets.

items.ask: Packaging isn't all made from the same card. Which kinds of board can you think of?
items.text: Corrugated, bleached, duplex, foil-backed, laminated and metal effect card; mount board; moulded paper pulp.

image.alt: A chair made from layers of corrugated cardboard, shown on a red display plinth.

check.q: What does 'compliant' mean for papers and boards?
check.a: They can be scored, folded and cut with basic tools, for example into nets for packaging.
Any three: layout, cartridge, tracing, bleed proof, treated, watercolour.

chunks.label: Composites
chunks.summary: Two or more materials combined for better properties.

items.ask: Why might combining two different materials give you something better than either one alone?
items.text: Two or more different materials combined, giving a material with enhanced properties.

image.alt: A cut-away drawing of a composite sheet, showing layers of fibres set inside the material.

items.ask: What could you set inside a plastic or cement to make it stronger?
items.text: Fibres set in another material, like CFRP, GRP or fibre cement.

image.alt: Close-up of dark woven carbon fibre fabric.

items.ask: What would you get if tiny hard particles were held together inside another material?
items.text: Particles held together in another material, like tungsten carbide or concrete.

image.alt: A block of grey material packed with many small teal particles of different sizes.

items.ask: How could thin layers be bonded together to make one strong material?
items.text: Layers bonded together, like aluminium composite board or glulam (engineered wood).

image.alt: The end of a laminated timber beam showing eight bonded layers, beside a panel with two thin metal skins on a thicker core.

check.a: Two or more different materials combined, giving a material with enhanced properties.

check.q: Name the three types of composite.
check.a: Fibre based, particle based and sheet based.

chunks.label: Smart and modern
chunks.summary: Materials that react to change, and new materials that don't.

items.ask: A mug changes colour when hot tea goes in. What kind of material is doing that?
items.text: Its physical properties change in response to an input like electricity, pressure, temperature or light.

image.alt: Coffee poured into a black mug beside a white mug whose face appears when it is hot.

items.ask: Which materials can you think of that change when they're heated, lit or pressed?
items.text: Shape memory alloys (SMA), thermochromic pigment and film, phosphorescent and photochromic pigments, electroluminescent wire, piezo electric material.

items.ask: If a material isn't found in nature, how might it come about?
items.text: Developed through new or improved processes, for example by human intervention.

items.ask: A material is new and high-tech. Does that make it smart?
items.text: Modern materials don't react to external change, so they are not smart materials.

items.ask: Which materials can you name that people have invented, rather than found?
items.text: Precious metal clay (PMC), Kevlar, high density modelling foam, polymorph.

check.a: Its physical properties change in response to an input or a change in its environment, such as electricity, pressure, temperature or light.

check.q: Why is Kevlar a modern material, not a smart one?
check.a: It was developed through new processes, but it doesn't react to external change.

keywords.def: A metal made mostly of iron and carbon; magnetic and will rust.
A metal that contains no iron; not magnetic and won't rust.
Two or more metals, or elements combined where at least one is a metal.
A polymer that can be reheated and reshaped again and again.
A polymer that forms rigid cross links when heated and can't be reshaped.
A polymer that deforms under pressure and returns to shape when released.
What holds a thermoplastic's long linear chain molecules together.
Can be scored, folded and cut with basic tools.
Two or more different materials combined for enhanced properties.
Its physical properties change in response to an input or the environment.
Developed through new or improved processes; doesn't react to change.

apply.q: A kitchen notice board must hold fridge magnets.
reasons: It is a ferrous metal, mostly iron and carbon, so it is magnetic
It contains no iron, so it will never rust
It is an alloy of two or more metals
It is a smart material that reacts to its environment

apply.q: The seal inside a water bottle lid must squash when the lid is screwed on, then spring back when it's opened.
reasons: An elastomer deforms under pressure and returns to its shape when released
A thermosetting polymer forms rigid cross links when heated
A thermoplastic can be reheated and reshaped again and again
A manufactured board comes in much larger sizes than solid wood

apply.q: A takeaway pizza box is cut from a flat net, scored and folded into shape.
reasons: A compliant material can be scored, folded and cut with basic tools
A hardwood comes from a broad-leafed, slow-growing tree
A sheet-based composite has layers bonded together
A thermosetting polymer can't be reheated and reshaped

oddOne.q: Which is the odd one out?

items.why: The only ferrous alloy: the rest contain no iron.
The only one made mainly of copper and zinc.
The only one based on tin.
The only one based on aluminium.

quiz.q: How many classifications of material are there for product design?
quiz.why: Metals, woods, polymers, papers and boards, composites, smart materials and modern materials.

quiz.q: In an exam answer, writing 'metal' is as good as writing 'low carbon steel'.
quiz.why: Always give the specific material's name, not just its classification.

quiz.q: Which of these is a ferrous metal?
quiz.why: Ferrous metals contain mostly iron and carbon; the others contain no iron.

quiz.q: Non-ferrous metals are magnetic and will rust.
quiz.why: Non-ferrous metals contain no iron, so they aren't magnetic and don't rust.

quiz.q: Brass is an example of…
quiz.why: Brass is an alloy with no iron in it, like bronze, duralumin and pewter.

quiz.q: What must an alloy always contain?
quiz.why: An alloy is two or more metals, or elements combined where at least one is a metal.

quiz.q: Cedar is…
quiz.why: Cedar comes from a coniferous tree, like pine, spruce, Douglas fir, redwood and larch.

quiz.q: Hardwoods come from broad-leafed (deciduous) trees.
quiz.why: Hardwood trees are broad-leafed, generally slow growing and lose their leaves in autumn.

quiz.q: Which of these is a manufactured board?
quiz.why: MDF is a man-made, wood-based composite; the others are solid woods.

quiz.q: Softwood trees are generally slow growing.
quiz.why: Softwoods are generally fast growing; hardwoods are the slow-growing ones.

quiz.q: Which type of polymer can be reheated and reshaped again and again?
quiz.why: That's why thermoplastics can be recycled after their first use.

quiz.q: What holds a thermoplastic's long linear chain molecules together?
quiz.why: Thermoplastics have long linear chains held by van der Waals forces; thermosets have rigid cross links.

quiz.q: A thermosetting polymer can be reshaped if it is heated to a very high temperature.
quiz.why: Its rigid cross links mean it can't be reheated and reshaped, even at very high temperatures.

quiz.q: Neoprene is an example of…
quiz.why: Neoprene, like natural rubber, polybutadiene and silicone, deforms under pressure and returns to shape.

quiz.q: Which of these is a thermosetting polymer?
quiz.why: Epoxy resin is a thermoset, like UF, MF and polyester resin; the others are thermoplastics.

quiz.q: A thermosetting polymer is a good choice for a product that will be recycled.
quiz.why: Thermosetting polymers can't be recycled, so they are the wrong choice.

quiz.q: Why are papers and boards called compliant materials?
options: They can be scored, folded and cut with basic tools
They react to changes in temperature
They come in larger sizes than solid wood
quiz.why: Being compliant is what lets them be made into items such as packaging nets.

quiz.q: Duplex card and mount board are classified as papers and boards.
quiz.why: Both are boards, in the same classification as papers such as layout and cartridge paper.

quiz.q: Glulam is which type of composite?
quiz.why: Glulam is an engineered wood made of layers, like aluminium composite board.

quiz.q: Tungsten carbide is a particle-based composite.
quiz.why: Tungsten carbide and concrete are both particle based.

quiz.q: What is a composite?
options: Two or more different materials combined for enhanced properties
A metal containing two or more elements
A material whose properties change with temperature
A wood from a broad-leafed tree
quiz.why: Combining the materials gives properties better than either alone. An alloy is a mix of metals.

quiz.q: Which of these is a smart material?
quiz.why: Thermochromic pigment reacts to temperature; the others are modern materials.

quiz.q: Modern materials react to changes in their environment.
quiz.why: Modern materials don't react to external change; that's why they aren't smart materials.

quiz.q: Kevlar is…
quiz.why: Kevlar was developed through new processes, like PMC, modelling foam and polymorph.

written.q: Explain how ferrous metals differ from non-ferrous metals. Name one example of each.
points: Ferrous metals contain mostly iron and carbon…
…non-ferrous metals contain no iron.
Ferrous metals are magnetic and will rust; non-ferrous metals are not magnetic and don't rust.
Ferrous example: low carbon steel, medium carbon steel or cast iron.
Non-ferrous example: aluminium, copper, zinc, silver, gold, titanium or tin.
written.model: Ferrous metals contain mostly iron and carbon, while non-ferrous metals contain no iron. Because of the iron, ferrous metals are magnetic and will rust; non-ferrous metals are not magnetic and don't rust. Low carbon steel is ferrous; aluminium is non-ferrous.
written.note: 1 mark per point, up to 4. Both examples are needed for an example mark.

written.q: Define the term 'composite' and name one example.
points: Two or more different materials combined…
…giving a material with enhanced properties.
Any named composite: CFRP, GRP, fibre cement, tungsten carbide, concrete, aluminium composite board, glulam.
written.model: A composite is made of two or more different materials combined, resulting in a material with enhanced properties. An example is carbon fibre reinforced plastic (CFRP).

points: Hardwoods come from broad-leafed (deciduous) trees; softwoods from coniferous (cone-bearing) trees.
Hardwood trees are generally slow growing; softwood trees are generally fast growing.
Hardwood trees lose their leaves in autumn; softwood trees tend to be evergreen.
Examples: hardwood such as oak, ash, mahogany, teak, birch or beech; softwood such as pine, spruce, Douglas fir, redwood, cedar or larch.
written.model: Hardwoods come from broad-leafed, deciduous trees, whereas softwoods come from coniferous, cone-bearing trees. Hardwood trees are generally slow growing and lose their leaves in autumn, while softwood trees are generally fast growing and tend to be evergreen. Oak is a hardwood; pine is a softwood.
written.note: 1 mark per comparison point; each point must cover both woods.

written.q: A drinks bottle will be collected and recycled after use. Explain why it should be made from a thermoplastic rather than a thermosetting polymer.
points: A thermoplastic can be reheated and reshaped again and again…
…so it can be recycled after its first use.
Heating a thermosetting polymer causes a chemical change that forms rigid cross links…
…so it can't be reheated and reshaped, and can't be recycled.
written.model: A thermoplastic can be reheated and reshaped again and again, so the bottle can be recycled after its first use. When a thermosetting polymer is heated, a chemical change forms rigid cross links between its molecules, so it can't be reheated and reshaped, which means it can't be recycled.
written.note: 2 marks for the thermoplastic, 2 for the thermosetting polymer: 1 for what it is, 1 for linking it to recycling.

written.q: Describe what is meant by a smart material and a modern material. Name two examples of each.
points: A smart material's physical properties change in response to an input or a change in its environment…
…such as electricity, pressure, temperature or light.
Two smart materials: e.g. shape memory alloy, thermochromic pigment or film, phosphorescent pigment, photochromic pigment, electroluminescent wire, piezo electric material.
A modern material is developed through the invention of new or improved processes, e.g. by human intervention.
Modern materials don't react to external change, so they are not smart.
Two modern materials: e.g. Kevlar, precious metal clay (PMC), high density modelling foam, polymorph.
written.model: A smart material is one whose physical properties change in response to an input or a change in its environment, such as electricity, pressure, temperature or light. Examples are shape memory alloy and thermochromic pigment. A modern material has been developed through the invention of new or improved processes, for example by human intervention. Modern materials don't react to external change, so they are not smart. Examples are Kevlar and polymorph.

written.q: Explain one reason why a designer might choose a manufactured board rather than solid wood for a large wardrobe side panel.
points: Manufactured boards are available in much larger sizes than solid wood…
…so the large panel can be cut from one sheet.
written.model: Manufactured boards are available in much larger sizes than solid wood, so the large side panel can be cut from one sheet.
written.note: 1 mark for the reason, 1 for linking it to the panel.
